utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Good afternoon, everybody. Could you please call the case. Good afternoon. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances, please. For the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner assisted by Ruth Karper, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and Mr. John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Before we start, we are eager to know what will be happening after we have heard our today's witness, probably today and tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't suppose it would be proper for me to say I am as eager to know as Your Honours are what's going to happen next. Your Honour, a number of difficulties have arisen. First of all, Mr. Inayat, not being aware that we were going to have this gap, is in fact not going to be here tomorrow. We had hoped that the video of the interview conducted with Dr. Stakic by the ITN news reporters would be available to be played this afternoon. The transcript, however, will not be ready, I understand, until 5.00. But it is possible that thereafter, we may be able to deal with that. It's about 45 minutes long. Your Honour, other than, that I'm afraid tomorrow we literally have no witnesses that we can call. The only -- Your Honour mentioned investigators yesterday. The only investigator outside Mr. Inayat who will be testifying is Mr. Nicolas Sebire, to deal with exhumations because his report is not yet complete because further information has been coming in. And that's why we can't -- and indeed, the Defence I don't believe has got a report from him. No, they haven't. So Your Honour, I'm very sorry. Normally, we are normally sort of having to send witnesses back. We've reached the stage now where we literally haven't got any witnesses to call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm afraid the Tribunal has reached a certain stage where problems arise due to the incredible workload of all the columns of this Tribunal. And it's easy to understand that things like this, unfortunately, happen. And you may have seen from the fact that the trial started a quarter later today, it's also for the Judges becoming an enormous problem to deal with eight cases at the same time in a responsible way. But we can't force the procedure in a not responsible way, and therefore, I believe we have to accept it. And I don't believe that there will be any objections by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections on our side, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, therefore, I think if -- I think maybe I've underestimated slightly how much longer, looking at the statement, it will take me to complete Mr. Atlija's evidence in chief. Looking at it, I see that -- of course I completely forgot the most important part that he had this conversation with Dr. Stakic -- allegedly had this conversation with Dr. Stakic. So I think it will probably take another hour to finish him in chief. Your Honour, the other matter is I'm going to ask him to look at the video that Your Honours saw with Mr. Inayat, S58, I believe, it has been produced as, of the area. He hasn't actually seen it before either. But it may help because it shows just the very small portions, about 2 or 3 minutes, if that, of the Brisevo area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. We can, after a few minutes we need for discussion of motions pending before us, we can then start. But please, allow me to emphasise that what you can read on the scheduling order distributed under today's date. I don't know whether you have received it already.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, we haven't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We, once again, as a kind of headline and initial remarks, the Trial Chamber emphasises that we invite the parties, nonetheless, that until now, there has been no agreement under Rule 62 ter of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence to try to come to a consensual solution in this case. And we note the paramount value of a consensual solution under the peacekeeping mission of this Tribunal. And we reemphasise, therefore, that the Trial Chamber remains prepared to assist the parties in any attempts to reach such a consensual solution, if they so want. And only for the purposes of a complete trial, this new scheduling order was needed. We discussed the dates yesterday. There were only two minor changes. As regards the finalisation of the Prosecutor's case, we had to substitute the 20th of September to the 19th of September, due to the technical reason that the 20th of September is already a courtroom maintenance day. And on the request of the Defence, the Defence case should resume January 8, 2003. Let me now turn, in a very open and frank way, to the request by the Prosecutor for the issuance of a subpoena duces tecum. First of all, we believe that within the Tribunal, it is not necessary to address one other institution of this Tribunal with the threat of a subpoena. And therefore, of course, I invite the parties for observations, we think it should be not necessary, and therefore an order only would be adequate. Then we have some doubts whether or not the Detention Unit is the correct addressee. Of course, it's no judicial person. It might be, but I leave it open for your observations, that the correct addressee is the Registrar, represented in this case by the Scheveningen Detention Unit, but the legal responsibility is vested with the Registrar possibly. I leave it open for discussion. As regards then the requested order itself, number 2 was not contested at all. There were some observations. As regards number 1. We will decide in detail these issues especially how far privileges in balancing have a predominant value to that what is for good reason sought by the Office of the Prosecutor. Nevertheless, it could be necessary, and I invite you for comments, it could be necessary to build in a second filter. As it reads now, the situation would be that the information would be provided from the Detention Unit directly to the Prosecutor. From our point of view, it could, worst case thinking, lead to the situation that privileged information, especially on the strategy of the Defence, would, by doing so, fall into the hands of the Prosecutor. This is not envisaged by the Prosecutor, no doubt. But the question is: How to have such a second filter? There is one possibility, and this is suggested that the documents, first of all, are packed and sealed and then unsealed in the presence of the Defence, the OTP, and an interpreter under the guidance and the decision of a third person. We discussed in length who could be this person, and we thought it's not possible to vest this work to one of the Judges working on this case. And therefore, our concrete question is whether or not the parties are prepared to accept that one of the four other ad litem Judges, members of the Trial Chamber 2 are vested with this decision whether or not a certain document, if disputed, falls under the categories where the limitations are applicable. But as to the fact that the rules, of course, do not provide for this situation, we would do this only with the consent of both parties, and therefore we invite the parties commenting on this special issue whether or not to vest this decisive function with another judge, an ad litem judge of this Trial Chamber. I invite your commentaries.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No objections to any of that. My only hesitation is in respect to who the order as opposed to a subpoena should be addressed. I know that we addressed it to the Detention Unit basing it on an earlier precedent. But if Your Honour is of the opinion, and which is shared by the Registrar, that he is the person who would deliver this from the Detention Unit, then we are perfectly content. Equally content to adopt the suggestion made by Your Honour as to the documents. I was, in fact, going to suggest that even the senior legal officer attached to the Chamber would be an appropriate person if Your Honour felt that. But I'm content that one of the other Judges should deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We have no objections to your proposal, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we'll hand down, as soon as possible, a decision on this matter. Anything else to be discussed before the witness appears? I can't see anything. The usher, could you please bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You feel prepared for a second round of questioning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. We are extremely grateful. And may the Prosecutor, please, start.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Atlija, yesterday you looked at a photograph of the area. I want you now to have a look at a video that was shot last year, and to see if you can help us by identifying relevant features. It may be -- I think if we let you watch it --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I say, Your Honour, it's very short.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Through first, and then go back and pick out the features.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I wonder if the audiovisual unit could play, it has been set up at the starting point until the screen goes blank. It's about 2 minutes' worth.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It has happened before, Your Honour, I'm sorry. We give it to the audiovisual unit set up to where we want to start it, and they take it back to the beginning. I'm not sure what's happening now. I'm sorry. Your Honour, I'm very sorry. It's my fault. I should have explained more carefully that I wanted to start where I had set it up. Could you go back -- could the audiovisual unit just run it back fast, and then I'll tell them where I want to start. Thank you. Okay. Stop. Thank you. Now, could you run it forward slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Could we go back then to where the we started just then. My apologies to the unit.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could we go back to where I started the video to where that bridge was. Could I also apologise to the unit because they were given the Court exhibit rather than the copy I was using. So it was my fault. So we go back to where that bridge was. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just pausing there for a moment, do you recognise the bridge, Mr. Atlija, at all?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This could be the bridge over the Sana at Ostra Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we move on, then, to the next bit, and I'll say "pause." Stop there, please. Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is the elementary school building in Ljubija. And another building adjacent to the football pitch of the Rudar Ljubija Football Club where the dressing rooms and the offices were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we move on, please. Could we pause for a moment. If you could stay "stop" when you require it, first of all, again, tell us as we've all seen, there's no sign, or very little, of where Brisevo was, where the village actually was, and also if I can indicate when the attack came, again, where it was coming from.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. What we've just seen now -- excuse me. What we have just seen were the remains of the iron ore mine, Ljubija, the so-called Tomeks Factory.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you run it back and say stop when you see it again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. We can see it in the middle of the screen, left of the road, the road can be seen clearly here in this tape.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. If we can carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Mr. Atlija, just say "stop" whenever you want to make a comment.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Stop. This is a part of the Raljas village, the hill you can see in the foreground. We call it Rivice Strane. That's when you go through Ljubija to Raljas in the direction of Brisevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we can see -- stop, please. I think we can see just one house. How many houses were there before?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say with any certainty, but more than one at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stop. What we're looking at now is a forest that goes down from Brisevo toward the Serb village of Rasavci. One of the directions by which the soldiers came was also from this forest.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. Can you please just rewind a bit. Stop. In the upper left corner of the screen, we can see a hill to which we came when the shelling of the village of Brisevo first started. We wanted to see where the shells were coming from. The altitude is about 490 metres. And on the right-hand side of the screen, it's not very clear, you can see the forest which descends to the village of Ostra Luka, which is another place the soldiers were coming from during that operation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes, if we can move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. Here in the foreground, we can see the remains of Andjelko Mlinar's and Nedo Mlinar's house. In the background, a bit -- it's a bit blurred, but you can see the remains of the remaining houses. They seem dots. Stop. In the upper right corner, you can see the remains of Janje Lovric's house. Stop. On the right-hand side, you can see the remains of the church. If you look straight from the church, looking to the foreground, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. there is the road for the hamlet of Marijana. I think we can see one, and then on the left-hand side of the screen, you can see a few more white dots which could be the remains of other houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before you move on, you told us how you were hiding whilst the soldiers came in and you were able to overhear what was said by the officers. Are we able to see roughly where you were hiding?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we just please rewind the image a bit, and then I'll show you. Stop. You can't see the exact spot here, but if we go from the remains of this house here, we can clearly see it, to the left down the slope, we would reach the precise spot. You can't see it here in this image, because it's behind the hill, and the house was on the other side of the hill but not on the top, but rather in the valley behind it so you can't see it in this film.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If a helicopter had flown over before the attack and subsequent destruction, would one have seen a number of houses in this shot?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, a number of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. If we just continue then, to the end again, please.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stop. On the right-hand side, the slope goes down towards a creek, and then goes up again, and then on that side, from Gornja Ravska and Ljubija, then members of the 5th Kozara Brigade came. Of course they didn't come in a single column. They were spread out, covering a large area. They didn't walk one behind the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can continue to the end, then.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stop. Stop. Here, we can see the centre of the village, but it's very difficult to discern where each of the houses were because of the orchards, and it was all in bloom when this was taken. So you can't see that much. If you head straight from where we're looking at now, we would reach the village of Stara Rijeka, Stari Majdan, and Sanski Most. And that's another direction the soldiers kept coming from, the soldiers of the 6th Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So around the ruins of the church which is now all field and, as you say, orchard, were there, in July of 1992, were there a number of houses?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can see a road leading from the church over the meadow to the left side. The Kresic family house and another house whose owners' last name was Mlinar was there. If we continue in the same direction, we would reach the houses of Sime Atlija and Joso Atlija. And then if we continue on, also Ante Atlija's house. If we head right from there, there were the houses, two houses belonging to the Marijan family. And then further on, the Ivandic family houses. But you can't see it in this film, not very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. All right.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stop. In the upper right corner of the image, you can see one of the houses. It's a white dot, a white sign. I think this house belonged to Srecko Dimac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stop. This is all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we can see that was the church. Do you want to go back?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to add that here, you can see the remains of the church and the house which belonged to Jozo Jakara. Perhaps I should also add that he was killed just below the house. You can see that there was a field, a meadow, below the house, and that's where his body was found.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Thank you very much. Thank you very much. That's it. Mr. Atlija, I want to deal now with what happened in the remaining period before you left of. After the main attack was over, and you've told us about the bodies that you were finding over the next few days or weeks, were there still armed men, soldiers, coming to Brisevo?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they kept coming, armed soldiers kept coming in smaller groups or individually.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When they came to Brisevo, what were they -- what was their purpose for the main part?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't ask them why they had come. We saw they were looting, and they set fire to the remaining houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Where any further people from Brisevo killed during this period?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ante Lovric, for instance, was killed then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see it. I heard it from his son. Several soldiers came from Ostra Luka and asked to buy a cow from him. He gave them the cow, and he told them that he should take it with them to Ostra Luka, and his sons then later found him in a woods between the villages of Brisevo and Ostra Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Anyone else, apart from him?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see myself, but from witnesses in Ljubija, it was said that someone by the name of Gavranovic was forced to crouch in the creek of Ljubija, and then he was shot in the head.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before I deal with where you were, can I ask you this: What happened to the women who remained in Brisevo?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the operation, the women were brought into one house that hadn't been burnt down. They were in a terrible state. Some of them wished to kill themselves. They were screaming, sobbing. And they had been raped and abused.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you see any of the women who had been raped subsequently?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did see some of them, but I didn't see any of those who had been raped.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you see the signs of any kind of injuries to any of the women?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Appreciating that you weren't there, do you know the sort of level of age or the rough ages of the women who were raped? I mean, were they young, middle-aged, old, or all types?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were of different ages. But as far as I knew, they were women of about 40 or 50 years old. There were younger ones and older ones, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, where did you, yourself, go after the attack?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Immediately after the attack, for a few days, we slept in the forest. We didn't dare sleep in any of the houses, and the women and the children slept in Ivica Dimac's house because it hadn't been burnt yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And where did you go after you had slept in the forest?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Afterwards, we divided up, and for some time I slept in Ljubija in Kukavica's house, a person by the name of Kukavica. He was an invalid. And he was not suspicious to the Serb soldiers. Others lived in the homes in Ljubija or in empty vacated houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to ask you next about a conversation or conversations you had with political and religious leaders. Do you recall a visit by Bishop Komarica from Banja Luka to Stara Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was he the head of the Catholic church for that particular area?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the archbishop of the Banja Luka area as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When he visited, was he accompanied by Vojo Kupresanin?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Vojo Kupresanin was with them, and Mr. Rasula, a person calling himself Nikola Gabelic. He said he was an official in the Banja Luka HDZ. And Mr. Anicic, who said that he was a manager or a representative of Caritas. I think his name was Miljenko Anicic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, can I ask you about Kupresanin. Did you know at the time who he was?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know who he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that the first time that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the first time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what position did you understand that he held?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he was a representative of the authorities, the authorities of the Serb Autonomous Region of Krajina. Whether he was president of that region or not, I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Rasula, do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know, but he said he was the president of the Serb Municipality of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you've already told us that Mr. Gabelic said that he was a member of the HDZ, I think you said, from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Mr. Anicic was a manager or representative of Caritas. Did you know at the time --

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What Caritas was?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew. I am a Catholic, and I knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I suppose most people do know, but can you just tell the Court. What was Caritas?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Caritas was a humanitarian organisation of the Catholic church.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, how did you find out about this particular visit?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Purely accidentally, with Jure Dimac I went to Sanski Most because my uncle had a house there and he had a telephone and I thought we might be able to telephone from his house. And then we saw a column of vehicles with police insignia, with red lights, and we saw someone wearing a bishop's clothes, robes. And when the column stopped in front of the church in Stara Rijeka, we decided to stay there, and we gave up our intention to go to Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So there you are in Stara Rijeka. Was there, then, an open meeting?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Several hundreds of people gathered, and an open meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's deal with what was said. Who began speaking?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the first speaker was Mr. Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what did he say to the assembled company, the people there?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He first introduced himself, and then he said that at the request of Bishop Komarica, he came with some people to find out what the situation was in the Sanska [as interpreted] and Prijedor areas were, what the relations between the Serbs and Croats were. He had heard about some incidents, and he said that before that, he didn't know that Croats lived in the area. And then he told us that we should not make war, but that we shall all live together as had been before. And that everything would be all right as soon as they established a Serb state in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you speak up at this meeting at all?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was one of the rare people who contradicted him. He said -- I told them that we were persecuted in the woods and everywhere, and then they expected us to live with them in peace. And we asked to be -- to let us leave from there, that the killings should stop, that if they wanted that territory, then they should keep it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you tell them, the dignitaries, that is, Kupresanin and the like, what had happened in your area?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I spoke in great detail about what had happened, and they listened to me until the end, until I finished, and they didn't interrupt me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: After you told them in detail what had happened, did Kupresanin reply to you?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kupresanin replied that such things occurred in wars, and that unfortunately, that a renegade group had committed that, and that we simply could not do anything about it and that he would see to it that we wouldn't be persecuted any more, or wouldn't be killed any more, and he would help us as much as he could.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us earlier when you were describing who took part in the attack, that Kupresanin had told you that it was the 6th Krajina Brigade. Was it at this meeting he told you that, or at a later meeting?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said it at that meeting, and he said that he would do everything in respect of General Talic so that the situation would end.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us that he said to you that it was a renegade group that had committed this. First, a renegade group from the 6th Krajina Brigade?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said that in that operation, that the operation, in fact, was not directed against us, but against the Muslims in the area, and that it had been carried out by the 6th Krajina Brigade and that all the killings had been done by a renegade group.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ask him anything about that statement that he had just made, that it was a renegade group?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him, how is it possible that one or two brigades should become renegade groups, and then he -- this provoked him, and he told me that I had better keep quiet.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did Bishop Komarica say anything during the course of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bishop Komarica also spoke at that meeting. He promised he would do everything for us, that humanitarian aid would be given to us, that food would be brought to us. He was very excited. He shouted at Vojo Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Kupresanin, and at the other people from the delegation. And I could conclude from what he had said that he hadn't been aware of what was going on earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Jumping ahead for a moment, do you know whether aid was provided to the people of Brisevo?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on a number of occasions, aid was provided.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: By who?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every time a truck would come with a driver escorted by Mr. Anicic. I mentioned his name before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So it came from Caritas, the aid?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you have any personal conversation with the bishop yourself that day?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had a talk with practically all the members of the delegation, including the bishop.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When the bishop left, was he alone in the vehicle in which he was?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was not alone. He was accompanied by people who were dressed in uniforms and with the JNA insignia on them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ask the bishop who these people were?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, during the second meeting, he said that he had been given bodyguards by General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, we can move to the second meeting. But I forgot to ask you this: Can you remember roughly when this meeting in Stara Rijeka was?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in August 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The end or the beginning, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it must have been the beginning of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you said that there was a second meeting. How long after this first one, roughly?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must have been three weeks following the first meeting. At the most a month after that first meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And where was that second meeting?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second meeting was at the Ljubija church.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who came to that second meeting?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I saw the Bishop Komarica, Mr. Vojo Kupresanin, and I didn't know the other members of the delegation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you speak to Mr. Kupresanin on that second occasion?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did speak with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was that just a personal conversation between the two of you, or again, was this in the context of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin invited me to the side and asked me if the situation had improved at all. When I said it hadn't, then he had a personal conversation with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was that conversation about?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about the general state of affairs there, and I asked him again to help us to move out from there and to go just about anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was his response when you asked for his help?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He promised he would help us to the greatest possible extent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did he offer any particular help in itself?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He offered specific help. He told us that from that day on, that we could telephone freely from the headquarters in Ljubija where Slobodan and Djoko Taranjac were the most important people there. And then he asked us to address Mr. Stakic, president of the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor. Mr. Savanovic, too, was mentioned in that context, and if he said if there were any problems that we should call him personally in Banja Luka, and he gave us the phone number.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, before I move to what you actually did do as a result of this assistance offered, can I just ask you this: You told us that you asked Bishop Komarica who the JNA uniformed men were, and he said they were Talic's bodyguards on that occasion, did you also speak to him about help as well?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did talk about health [as interpreted] as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I thought you said "help," not "health." Sorry.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, help, help.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it came up on the screen as health. That's what I heard through my earphones. What was his reaction when you were asking him for help, other than the aid from Caritas, did you ask him for any other sort of help?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bishop Komarica was against us moving from there. He told us that these were our homes of 700 years back, that we should preserve our parish, to try to live there, to continue living there, and words to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what did you say when he tried to persuade you to stay?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We told him, well, these homes are worthless if we will be killed there. And people are what are important, the parish itself isn't important. We can live anywhere else, even in Australia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kupresanin had told you to address Mr. Stakic, president of the Municipal Assembly, and also he had mentioned a Mr. Savanovic. As a result of that, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a few days, we went to the Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: How many of you went?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Who were the other two people?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zdenka Lovric. Now married, and her last name is Dimac. And Jure Dimac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when you went to the Prijedor Municipality, who did you see there?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the entrance to the building, there was a porter who asked us where we were going, and then he asked us to leave our weapons, if we had any, with him. So he was the first person we met.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, this is the way it came out on the screen. By the municipality, do you mean the municipality building?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. At the entrance of the building, there was a porter, a guard standing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And he asked if you had any -- to leave your weapons. Once you got inside the building -- sorry. Did you ask to see anybody in particular when you got there?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We said that we had to go to Mr. Stakic. He told us that if we had any weapons, we should leave them with him, and then he let us in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Had you made an appointment to see Mr. Stakic in advance?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the meeting had been arranged by phone, by the brothers Taranjac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you get in to see Mr. Stakic, then?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told us that we should go to the first floor of that building. In front of the office, there was a table and a few chairs. We were told to wait there, and then a woman came and she took us to an office. And in that office, there was a gentleman we expected was Mr. Stakic, because we had the meeting scheduled with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Had you seen Mr. Stakic before, on television or in real life?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had never seen him before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The man who was sitting there, did he tell you who he was?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether he told us what his name was or what his post was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said the man you expected to be was Mr. Stakic, that you had expected to see there, was Mr. Stakic. Did you actually meet Mr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That gentleman who was sitting in the office, well, we had a meeting with him, and I am convinced that it was Mr. Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What convinces you of that? Did he tell you his name?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly whether he told us his name. But through our conversation, the gentleman kindly listened to us, and then said that he could only help us by helping us not to sleep in forests and in houses that had been destroyed, but that we should move into abandoned houses in Biscani. And that as far as moving was concerned, that he couldn't help us there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Can we then go back to the beginning of this conversation. How did it begin? Did you speak, or did he speak?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told us to sit down, and then he asked us what we came to see him for and what we had to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And so what did you tell him?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We said we were from Brisevo and sent to see him by Mr. Kupresanin, that we would like to ask him to help us to move out, to leave that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you tell him where you wanted to go?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We said we had relatives in Germany, Croatia, Austria. It didn't matter; the only thing that really mattered was to leave that area where war was still raging.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what did he respond when you said you wanted help to leave the area?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said he was not able to help us to leave the area because they were being accused of ethnic cleansing already at that point and that the only thing he could do for us was to put us up in those houses that were still whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did he say anything to you about houses, whereabouts those houses were?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the village of Biscani was mentioned, and we knew where the village was, so there was no need for him to explain to us where those houses were, because we knew the location of that village.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did he tell you what had happened in Biscani?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing specific really. He only told us that we could go there and occupy the empty houses in Biscani.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did he mention your own town of Brisevo at all, or own village?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember that he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. When he was offering you the houses in Biscani, did he say why it will be a good idea for you to go and live there?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in that sense, he didn't say anything. He only told us we could go there because those houses were not that damaged, and that it was better for us to stay in those houses without a roof over our heads or in houses that had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you were telling him what had happened to you, how much knowledge did the man you were talking to appear to have, as to what had happened in Biscani and in Brisevo?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find it difficult to say now, how much someone else knew, but I think he must have known that Biscani had been vacated, as he made the offer to us to go there and stay there. Had he not known that the village was empty, probably he wouldn't have made the offer that he did for us to move there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did he show any knowledge from what he said, the words he used, of what had actually taken place in Brisevo itself?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he must have known what had occurred there, and I think the other officials in Prijedor Municipality and Sanski Most Municipality must have known.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. But was there anything that he said to you that showed a knowledge of what had happened, the attacks or the burnings or anything like that, not whether he must have known, or did he indicate it to you by what he said?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't ask about any details about the events in Brisevo. He didn't inquire why we had no houses of our own to sleep in. So that sort of led me to conclude that he must have known what had happened there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, how did the meeting end then?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We said thanks and said that we were not inclined really to accept his offer, and that we would keep on trying to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: During the course of this meeting, was there anybody, any other officials in the room with you?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not for the whole duration of the meeting, but I think there was another gentleman who kept coming in and out. It all lasted for a very short time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you told the porter that you had an appointment to see Mr. Stakic. Did the man who you spoke to ever say who he was?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regrettably, I can't remember whether he spoke to us and told us his name in the sense of saying "my name is Stakic" or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If the man had said "I am not Mr. Stakic," would you have done anything about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the fourth time, really. My learned friend is asking the same question. I think the witness answered clearly that the gentleman on the opposite side of the table has never mentioned his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I accept that, and that's why I'm changing it slightly -- the question I asked is not the same question. So I would ask that I get an answer to that, or I was starting to ask before I was interrupted, or maybe I did ask. Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If the man it said "I'm not Mr. Stakic," would you have done anything about it?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably I would have asked him why he had agreed to see us in the first place because our meeting was supposed to be with Mr. Stakic. But he never told us that he was not Mr. Stakic. I can't remember him saying that either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Finally, then, did you, in fact, manage to leave the area for Zagreb on the 17th of November of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before you were able to leave, did you have to do anything in terms of paperwork or payment?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had to pay the electricity, phone, and other utility bills. There was no phone in Brisevo, let me just make that clear. So we paid for a number of things that we never used.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you have to sign any documents before you left?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were supposed to sign that we were leaving of our own free will, and then also sign a certificate leaving our property at the disposal of -- I can't remember whether it was called Republika Srpska or the Autonomous Region of Serbian Krajina at that point. I can't say with certainty now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how did you actually leave, physically leave, the area?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I joined a convoy, an organised convoy, organised with the consent of the Serb authorities but also with the assistance of the UNHCR and the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And where did the convoy cross into -- out of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was at the Bosanska Gradiska, Stara Gradiska border crossing. That part of Croatia was then controlled by the UN, and it was called the UNPA zone. But I don't know what it was marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before the convoy was allowed to leave, did any search take place, in Gradiska, that is?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the bridge in Gradiska, all the men had been taken out. We were told to take out our luggage, and then the luggage was searched. And the pockets of the men were searched, too, but they never touched the women and children.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The search was conducted by whom?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were Serb soldiers, but there were also persons wearing the blue police uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What happened if people had money or valuables on them?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took money from some people, but they didn't take anything from me, for one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Atlija, thank you very much, if you'd like to wait there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: In fact, you don't have any other questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't have any other questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. What's the timeframe the Defence needs for starting the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We just can have a break, Your Honour, and we'll be ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The trial stands adjourned until 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. The Defence may start the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hello. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We both speak B/C/S as the language is called here, Bosnian, Croatian, Serbian, so this may cause a bit of trouble because our questions and answers may overlap at times. So, I would please ask you if you can just make a pause after my question, you can see it on your screen when the interpretation is completed, so that no additional trouble is caused to the interpretation service.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There will be no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will follow the line of questioning pursued by the Prosecution yesterday, and of course I will not go into as much detail as my colleague yesterday. Of course, I will not ask you anything about the events that must have caused you great pain, and we shall not go into any particulars surrounding the graves or the unfortunate events when your father was killed. I will only ask you to please assist us in clarifying a number of issues that we think you could help us with, in order to further clarify these issues. On page 9 -- let me just inform you, please, it is for the sake of the transcript that we must always give the number of page and the line where you made a certain statement. Please do not be confused by this. On page 9, line 21 of the transcript, you were speaking about the repeater being taken. Before the taking of the repeater, could you follow the programmes of both the Zagreb and the Sarajevo studios?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we could.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Before the repeater was taken, was there any propaganda in those programmes?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was, but in my opinion, to a far smaller extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 12, line 4, you spoke about the fact that most of the armed people who moved about were Serbs. Are you familiar with the fact that in the Prijedor municipal area, a mobilisation had been carried out in September and November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with that, because I was called up myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you respond to the callup?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there was an additional mobilisation in 1992?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know anything about any such details.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm only asking you to answer what you can. Those mobilisations, were the majority of the people who did respond to these callups Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The majority of those people you saw who were armed, were they wearing military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, most of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During that period, do you know if the JNA was the legitimate military power in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say precisely until which date exactly the JNA indeed was the legitimate military power in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the JNA a legitimate power prior to the takeover on the 30th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 13, line 21, you spoke about the need to be in possession of permits to move about. In order to be able to move about freely at all around the Prijedor municipal territory. Do you know whether Serb civilians also needed to have -- needed to be in possession of these permits in order to be able to move about freely, especially men of military age and men capable of military service?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I only know that we non-Serbs had to have these permits in order to move about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if those Serbs who were fit for military service were allowed to leave the Autonomous Region of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 14, the beginning of the page, you spoke about Milan Mutic, who moved into your flat in Prijedor. After the war, did you ask for this flat to be returned to you?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The procedure is underway, and it's all in the hands of my lawyers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that people were also moving into flats abandoned by Serbs, which had been owned by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but my flat had not been abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that someone was actually living in your flat?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I left to go to my parents' house, that did not necessarily mean that I had left my own flat for good, never to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the same page, page 14, line 18, you spoke about May 1992 when the refugees came from Hambarine in great numbers to your village. Do you know, because you have yourself said that they stayed for several days, whether after that period, some of them did eventually return to Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, some of them went back to Hambarine, and the others dispersed. And most of them I think went to Stari Majdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page 15, you spoke about a conflict at the checkpoint in Hambarine and the request for Aziz Aliskovic to surrender and some other people alongside with him. Do you know if Aziz Aliskovic actually surrendered?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that he did not surrender, because I saw his dead body brought to Ljubija later on. He was killed later on at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As concerns the conflict at the checkpoint, do you really know what happened there, or only from accounts by other people?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only from the accounts of other people, because I did not witness this myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On page 17, line 4, you spoke again about the group of refugees from Hambarine. You said that most of those people were women, children, the elderly, but that there were also some young men among them.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is indeed what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know where the other men from Hambarine were at that time?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no way for me to know where the other inhabitants of Hambarine were at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did those women and all the men there tell you where the other men were?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They said that some of them had tried to put up resistance, but they failed, and they dispersed and ran to several different places.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether those men later retreated to the Kurevo forest?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard stories later on that there were such men indeed who hid in the Kurevo forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Atlija, do you know that the Autonomous Region of Krajina for a while was completely cut off from Yugoslavia, and have you heard about fighting for the corridor?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about those fights, but I can't accept the fact that some Autonomous Region of Krajina was ever cut off from any state. The recognised state at that point was Yugoslavia, as far as I can remember, and to the best of my knowledge, no autonomous regions had ever been recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're not speaking about the legal aspect. I'm talking about the physical area that was then referred to as the "Autonomous Region of Krajina" but you have answered my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear on the radio several times about the fighting going on for the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that at one moment in Bosnia, there was a situation where everyone fought everyone else? For example, when in Herzegovina, Serbs fought Croats, and at the same time the Muslims, for example, attacked the Croats in the Travnik region?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to ask how that's relevant, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that next to your village, there were also other settlements where the pop -- where the Croatian population was in the majority or totally Croatian.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, you mentioned Ravska and Zune, and Gornja Ljubija. Were these -- had these places been destroyed like your own village, or did they have another fate?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were destroyed to a far lesser extent, and there were far fewer casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us now, and you mentioned this today on page 18, line 4 of today's transcript, how often did the Caritas trucks with humanitarian aid come to your village?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once -- twice or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the transcript, it says "once, twice, or three." Can we agree that you said two or three times?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree that there may be a misunderstanding. The trucks coming -- did not always come to Brisevo. Sometimes they came to Stara Rijeka. So this may have caused a misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Atlija, I have just completed my cross-examination, and I hope Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that you didn't have any problems in providing answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for providing these answers. Nevertheless, in the beginning, I have one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever see photos of some of the persons you met, for example, the bishop, the archbishop, people from Caritas or other people you saw during the meeting, on television or in newspapers?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw on television, in the papers the bishop, Mr. Komarica, and perhaps Mr. Miljenko Anicic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And what about the other persons you mentioned during your examination, Mr. Kuruzovic, for example, or others.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was Kupresanin, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry, Kupresanin, Vojo. I'm thinking first names. Kupresanin, sorry.

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on I didn't see them any more, because I went to Germany. I had many private problems, and I was not very concerned by that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Did you ever see Dr. Stakic again?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards Mr. Stakic, I heard about him, but I saw him the first time yesterday when I entered the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When you entered the courtroom, were you immediately sure that this was the person you have met in the municipality building in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is that person, but I must say that it is very difficult after a period of ten years to be truly sure of someone who had -- I had only seen once in my life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. I know this from my own experience. It's extremely difficult, but sometimes one reflects, for example, in the evening. Something may have changed with the face one saw or, yeah, the impression one had from a person. No doubt, it's a totally different environment whether you are here in this courtroom or in Prijedor. No doubt about this. Did you try to find out, has something changed?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I kept thinking about this and whether the person had introduced himself when we went to his office. I remember very well that he was wearing civilian clothes, and I was struck by that because at the time, most people wore military clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Dr. Stakic, of course, you are not obliged to do so, but in consultation with your Defence counsel, if you so want, may you please stand up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we can just have a minute to caucus, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If the Court can just, please, restate the question, and we'll proceed accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The question is if Dr. Stakic would be so kind just to stand up. Could you please be so kind and, if you so want, approach Dr. Stakic and try to look in his eyes and try to find out whether you can today, by the one or other reason, identify Dr. Stakic. Dr. Stakic, you may be seated, please. What is your impression, please tell us?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I had met Mr. Stakic in the building of the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: When you say "Mr. Stakic," then it's the person you just approached here in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I refer to that person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Atlija. Any more questions? Judge Fassi Fihri? No. Judge Vassylenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Yes, I have some. Mr. Atlija, you said in your written statement of October, year 2000, page 4, English version, during the election campaign of 1990, the media started to inflame the situation by inciting Serbs through propaganda against non-Serbs. Serbs had complete control over the media in our region namely, Prijedor and Banja Luka. Can you be more specific about the persons who were engaged or involved in this propaganda activity? Had you seen them on the TV screens? Have you heard them on the radio, or have you read the newspapers, and can you single out the particular persons engaged in propaganda?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was a journalist of Radio Prijedor and of the Kozara Vjesnik, Milan Mutic, not the person who moved into my apartment. But the names of the others, I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: On page 13 of your written statement, you mentioned the existence of the Serb Radical Party of Seselj, and refer to Nikola Marinovic as one of the officials of this party. Do you know other officials of this party in Prijedor Municipality, at that time, of course? Or active members of this party?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the names of the officials. There were some people who were in the central repair shop and who boasted that they were members of the Serbian Radical Party. They had their insignia, their marks, and their propaganda material with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: While testifying before the Croatian Information Centre in January of 1993, you said that the president of - it's page 12, English version - "the president of Prijedor Municipality Stakic and his deputy Savanovic ordered us to move to Biscani to cover up the massacre they had committed in that Muslim village." Can you be more specific about who ordered, in what form you were ordered to move to Biscani to cover the massacre?

utterances.speaker: IVO ATLIJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the talk we had with Mr. Stakic, we concluded that the only reason why we were sent to Biscani, and why we were not allowed to move out of Bosnia and Herzegovina, was that they wished to conceal the crimes that happened in that village. I would like to mention that at that time, the representative of the United Nations was supposed to come to the area. He engaged in human rights. I think his name was Mazowiecki. I believe that the two things might have been connected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Atlija. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I then ask the parties if there are any questions emanating from the questions of the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think it's more for the Defence, but can I mention this: I notice that there was no cross-examination at all on the content of the meeting that they had at the municipal building. I was going to ask whether there was any dispute, because as I say, that ought to be put. But I concluded that because it was fair for the Defence to address you at any later stage on the basis that it was not shown that this was Mr. Stakic. But in the light of what's now happened, I don't know whether Your Honours might feel it would be helpful to know whether there is any dispute about that conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's the right of the accused, and therefore also of the Defence counsel, to remain silent on this issue, if they so want. Of course, it's your right to put questions if you so want now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, it's not a matter of a right to remain silent. It's a matter of taking the direct testimony that was offered by this witness and examining it in its entirety. If counsel is unsatisfied with the answers she obtained, it's not our job or the Court's job or anyone's job to rehabilitate the witness or to extract other questions. The gentleman gave us what he believes was his best recollection. We should not be even discussing this in front of the witness, number one. Number two, we should not be discussing positions of the parties after each witness, as the OTP now has consistently done on the last three witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask you that we discuss these issues in the absence of the witness. And in addition, I don't want to allow you to use verbs like "rehabilitate" a witness. This is not the appropriate language. I think we have to be all grateful that the witness before us tries the best of his own knowledge to tell us what he has experienced in the past. And it was extremely difficult for this witness, and therefore we should be grateful. And we are. Let's please discuss this in the absence of the witness. If you have any further questions to the witness, please do it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We do not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Then this concludes --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honour, I think it maybe as well as the witness is asked to withdraw to the witness room. I take Mr. Ostojic's point about discussing this matter in front of the witnesses. But I don't think, with the greatest of respect to Mr. Ostojic, and that's because of the jurisdiction --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I don't think we should continue discussing this here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no, I'm simply going to say, we need to discuss this, and it may be the witness will have to come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Mr. Atlija, I'm awfully sorry for this, but could you please be so kind and be prepared to come back, if necessary, after our next break. And it is not necessary, then already now, I want to express my gratitude that you have been here and give us your testimony. You're excused, but please wait until you get the information that it's not necessary for you to come back. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So I interrupted first Mr. Ostojic. And therefore, Mr. Ostojic has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Obviously, if the Defence wished to attack the credibility of this witness, we would have done so. We accepted what the witness said. We find it quite offensive that the OTP, after every witness when they call seemingly most recently that they want to have, in essence, a summary session as to whether the witness was a plus or a minus witness for them, and or a plus or a minus witness with certain elements within the counts of the fourth amended indictment. It's not appropriate for us to respond at this time. We will have our opportunity, as we, under the rules of this Tribunal, have to call witnesses who are either present at the meeting, witnesses who knew about the meeting, if we wish to contest that. We're under absolutely no obligation to tell the OTP now, and when I said "rehabilitation", Your Honour, quite frankly it wasn't a disrespect to the witness. That's why we didn't challenge him about his recollection of the events. It's the OTP who's concerned about it and the OTP who seem to be unsatisfied with what the witness said, both in his statement and then on the witness stand under oath, and was unsatisfied and hoped that more could be extracted from that. The witness said what we think were rather benign and perhaps even helpful things during his testimony for the Defence, and that's why we choose to question him only in the limited fashion that we did. But I will not, unless the Court instructs us obviously, have a discussion with the OTP after each and every witness, after each and every cross-examination, if a witness was in favour of one point or not. That's for the Judges to decide, after hopefully hearing our arguments on those issues from both parties. I would gladly debate it with the OTP, but I don't think it's either a requirement nor is it necessary at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. I just have to emphasise that when we are using words such as "rehabilitation," then for us, it may be sound different than to a witness before us, being not acquainted with our language. And therefore, in the presence of the witness, I wanted, and I had to, avoid any kind of misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour is absolutely right, because the word "rehabilitates" suggested that the witness had in some way been reduced from being a credible witness. Now, Your Honour, this is a discussion, let's put it as its lowest, that we have had particularly with those who practice in the American jurisdiction. The American jurisdictions do not insist that the terms of Rule 90 [H] (ii) are followed. Mr. Ostojic is deliberately, in my view, deflecting what is a simply straightforward concept into the OTP's apparent, as it were, wish to try and get round answers given or the like. The rule says very clearly: "In the cross-examination of a witness who is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party, counsel shall put to that witness the nature of the case of the party for whom that counsel appears, which is in contradiction of the evidence given by the witness." Now, in normal circumstances, Your Honour, I would, of course, accept that if there's no cross-examination to suggest that something different was said or that something different happened, it was accepted. But because I know, because I have had this discussion endlessly with other counsel in other cases in this Tribunal, that is not the practice in some jurisdictions. In order to ensure that everybody is, as it were, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. singing from the same hymn sheet, I have now raised it twice in this Court. In this particular case, evidence was given by this witness of a conversation with a person at the highest who didn't say he was Mr. Stakic, and I accept that. However, after Your Honours intervened and asked him to look at Dr. Stakic, he said: "Yes, I think that's the man I saw." In that event, Your Honour, all I wanted to know was whether, given we had moved slightly from that position, otherwise it would have been open to the Defence to say at the end of the day: "There's no proof that the man that they talked to this was Dr. Stakic, and that's why we didn't need to cross-examine, but in fact, our case on that is different. We're going to say, either through the evidence of Dr. Stakic or somebody else who was there, that that's now how the conversation went." If that's the case, they have an obligation, which the Appeals Chamber has made absolutely plain, to put to the witness there and then, and not wait until the Defence case for it suddenly to emerge that not "you're lying," but "can we put it to you, Mr. Atlija, your recollection of that conversation is wrong." That's all that I'm saying. If, however, it's accepted that that conversation with Dr. Stakic happened in that way, then, of course, they don't have to put it. And that's the only point that I'm making. And I hope that's now clear to Mr. Ostojic and to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Of course I will, and I have to refrain, from commenting on this. One point for me seems to be quite clear: If the accused and the Defence counsel don't do anything else than representing Dr. Stakic and therefore, exercising the rights of Dr. Stakic, if they decide to remain silent, not to cross-examine, sometimes for good reason, in one case, for the good reason of the protection of a witness, then this has to be accepted, and we can draw inferences only from that what we can read from the transcript. And we can't say that by not cross-examining a witness, everything is no longer contested what the witness has said. It is of course the good right of the Defence to establish their case and, thereby, questioning whether each and every word a witness has said was indeed correct. And I don't think we should go into further discussion of this question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm very sorry. Of course, I haven't made it clear either, then. Of course not each and every word that a witness said may be agreed. But on vital matters, Your Honour, I do submit that here we do have a clear Appeals Chamber ruling that, for example, on a conversation or an act that is specific or material, if at a later stage in the Defence case, evidence will be called either through the defendant -- the accused himself or through other evidence, there is an obligation, a duty, under the rules for that to be put to the witness which it concerns while that witness is here. Your Honour, on that one, it may be a departure from other jurisdictions, but the Appeals Chamber last month said that must happen. And for obvious and good reason. It does not -- it is not an abrogation. They dealt with that in terms. "It's not an abrogation of the accused's right of silence or the accused/client confidentiality between the accused and his lawyers to have to put to a witness if his evidence on a material matter is not accepted."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please understand that I continue saying that I am not prepared to discuss these legal issues, especially not when you try to discuss my own words in the Kunarac decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I wasn't aware that I was discussing Your Honour's own words in the Kunarac decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think there was only one judgement in the last month from the Appeals Chamber. Right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm talking about the decision on this rule that came down. I said the last month, it may now be longer. In the Brdjanin/Talic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
