utterances.text: I'm aware of this. And even in the light of this what you are referring now to, I think the opinions have been exchanged, and it's for the Judges at the end of the day, after having heard both cases, to decide on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. It's my fault, then. I wasn't aware that issue had come up in the Kunarac appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I was surprised to hear. If you didn't want to mention questions on errors of fact or fact-finding in Kunarac, then it's fine. If you want to -- because you said "a decision of the Appeals Chamber in the last month," and I therefore you immediate reference to the Kunarac judgement.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I wasn't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Now you made it quite clear that you make reference to Brdjanin/Talic. And I'm aware of this decision there. But nevertheless, you can't bring Judges in the middle of a case to a decision on this matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, and I hope Your Honour will forgive me. I don't mean to -- but it's such an important principle, this. Your Honour, I know that the judgement came out when this case has already started. But the Trial Chambers and counsel who practice before them are bound by the decisions of the Appeals Chamber, because if they are not, then the Appeals Chamber might just as well not deliver decisions. And this is such a fundamental principle of such importance because the main reason, Your Honour I don't want to rehearse it, the main reason is that what has been happening historically was the Defence case would start, and suddenly all kinds of matters, material matters would be challenged in the Defence case, which had never been put to the witnesses in the Prosecution case. And that's the real matter of importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think if I may, the Defence has reviewed the materials and the rules, and I think we are hopefully capable enough to withstand anything that the OTP will throw. But I find it odd that on one hand they want us to challenge everything, but why doesn't Ms. Korner challenge this witness when he says that he saw Mr. Stakic, and he was the president of the Municipal Assembly. Why doesn't she call him a liar and say it's not true that he was only president, that he was the head of the National Defence Council, he was the head of the Crisis Staff, et cetera, et cetera. Or is she withdrawing all those allegations in the fourth amended complaint. Why we are even having this discussion is beyond reason for me quite frankly. The Defence has prepared our cross. Quite frankly I think we were cut off from questions that were direct to the witness because we wanted to not be as confrontational to the witness on certain points. And without a basis, Your Honour, as I hope you have all seen, we do not simply go to a witness and test their veracity by simply telling them that they are being untruthful or simply as the OTP has said, lying. What we have tried to do is find inconsistencies in their prior testimony as well as in their prior statements. And I think we have accomplished that. The OTP should, in turn, now if they want to act in good faith, take their witnesses and show the Court and the Defence that they are going to amend their indictment and reduce some of the far and overreaching allegations that they have set forth in that indictment by their very own witnesses. And the OTP would like to share with us what is it in that conversation that they claim is vital or important, to what elements will it go to, let them read the decisional authority regarding deportation and what the elements are, and how what this gentleman said under oath on the stand, how they may or may not fit within the counts concerning deportation. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, but this is what I'm talking about. This is right off the point, the very simple point I'm making. What has the indictment got to do with this? What does all of this got to do with the point I'm making? Apart from the fact, we can't cross-examine our own witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think they have, quite frankly, Your Honour, and I think they have more than we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm not prepared to let this debate continue. I'm quite sure both parties even if we are all from different jurisdictions, and we all are acquainted with different systems, we know about the basic rules, the rules in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence before us, the jurisprudence of the Strassbourg Court and other authorities relevant for our decisions, and we are aware of the jurisprudence of the Appeals Chamber, and I think none of the parties should try to challenge that the other party is not aware of these decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will have one -- can I just very briefly have one last point. Your Honour, I don't know. That's a matter of comment and argument at the end of the day as to whether this conversation, as related by the witness is of assistance to the Prosecution or the Defence, or indeed Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's for the Judges. And I hereby end this dispute. Are there any other contributions? I heard that there would be a videotape to be played by the OTP. Is it correct? Is it prepared?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not ready, I'm told. Is that right? Mr. Koumjian is here to deal with this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: My understanding is it's ready now. It has to be picked up. It just was prepared about 5 minutes ago, as far as a copy being made. I just want to make sure that the Defence has no objections to us playing it at the present time. This is a video that we disclosed about six weeks ago, after the trial started, that we obtained a day or two before we disclosed it to the Defence. It's an interview with Dr. Stakic. It's about 47, 48 minutes long. And the transcript was just prepared, the English transcript today. So today, we obtained the English transcript. We could play that today, tomorrow. But we do not have any other witnesses for this week. Just wanted Your Honours to know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Let me first check --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sorry. Let me first come back. We have still a witness waiting outside. There was a possibility now for both parties to rethink whether or not there are additional questions to the witness. May I ask first the OTP, any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Only the point that I just made --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] We don't have any further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the usher please tell the witness that he's excused. And once again, with our gratitude. I think in order -- it's also as understood correctly, the interest of the parties not to have an additional hearing tomorrow, it would be appropriate to have a break of half an hour now, and then follow the video provided by the OTP. I can see nodding from both sides. Then we proceed as foreseen. The trial stands adjourned until 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. May we please proceed. The OTP has prepared a video, and we are grateful to have received a translation transcript of interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We do have a videotape. I'm prepared to make -- if Your Honours would like, briefly describe where we got it from, but I think it's rather self-authenticating. It's an interview with the accused I would ask that the tape, the B/C/S and the English transcript, be marked as exhibits for the next number in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN

I wrote a letter to Channel 4 of British television asking for outtakes, that is, items of the interview that were not broadcast. Part of this interview was broadcast publicly, and has appeared in other videos, perhaps even in this Court. But we asked for the entire tape of the interview. That's what we obtained, after this trial had already started. The transcript that I asked for, in the interview you'll see that the report asks questions in English, apparently has an interpreter sitting next to him. The interpreter then interprets that question into B/C/S, and Dr. Stakic answers in B/C/S, and the interpreter whispers the answer in English to the reporter. So in the audiotape you will not hear the English and will need to have an English translation simultaneous to the tape. I would also ask that the English booth, at any time if they need to catch up, that they just indicate stop so that the tape could be stopped, if that's necessary. The transcript that you have, that I asked for, when it indicates Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. "reporter," I asked that that actually be what the interpreter is saying to Dr. Stakic, because I think the key question is the question that he understood, So, "reporter" is what the B/C/S interpreter asked Dr. Stakic and then the "Stakic" is Dr. Stakic's answers. utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. May it please be started.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Dr. Milomir Stakic, president of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly. "Reporter: What is the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor? "Stakic: It is the highest legislative organ in the territory of Prijedor municipality. "Reporter: Is that something like the mayor of Prijedor? "Stakic:, yes, precisely that. "Reporter: What responsibilities, obligations, do you have? "Stakic: My obligations are to implement the decisions that are adopted by that organ, the Municipal Assembly. According to the rules of procedure, I convene the Municipal Assembly, draft the agenda, which can, again, at the intervention of a certain number of deputies in the assembly be changed, expanded, and so on. Essentially, I implement the decisions of the Municipal Assembly, and put my signature on those decisions. "Reporter: And how long have you been in this post? "Stakic: I have been in that post for six months, seven months already, even longer. Longer. "Reporter: And before that? "Stakic: I was the vice-president of the Municipal Assembly. "Reporter: Before that you were the vice-president of the assembly? "Stakic: Yes. "Reporter: What is the situation like today in Prijedor? "Stakic: Considering the war in, in our territories, the territories of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina, the situation in Prijedor and in the territory of the Prijedor Municipality itself, is quite good. Quite good considering the war. With the exception of individual cases or smaller groups of saboteurs and those who crop up, extremists left behind in the forests of Kozara and on the slopes of Grmec, we have no other problems as far as the war is concerned. A good number of our people are in the Army of Republika Srpska, defending the territory of Republika Srpska. However, Prijedor as a municipality, is surrounded by the municipalities of Gradiska, Dubica, Krupa, Sanski Most, and Banja Luka, where it is also peaceful, where the situation is satisfactory, so that in our territory, we do not have those large-scale war conflicts and occurrences. However, the problems are of a different nature. There is no heating, which you can see yourselves. There are shortages of medicines, food, and other consumer goods in the shops. Electricity. We are fortunate today. The supply is a little better, and so we can even film this. And numerous other problems that accompany all these occurrences, because the shortage of electricity, petroleum, and petrol products prevents the economy from operating so that we are operating at only 10 to 15 per cent of the capacities and trying to survive with that. "Reporter: What is most difficult to get here that people need? "Stakic: At present, the biggest problem is mazout. I am just coming from a meeting with all the directors of firms, both private and socially owned ones, in the Prijedor Municipality area where we succeeded in finding some sort of solution to finance the purchasing of mazout, however, our only way out to the world it through the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and there is an embargo on transit through Yugoslavia. So even though we have paid for and signed contracts for quantities in certain European countries, we cannot get them. And I was forced to ask the UN High Commissariat for Refugees and the High Commissariat of the Red Cross to try to use their influence among responsible persons in the European Community and the United Nations to procure a paper, a certificate, for the import of this mazout. We will pay for it, but we need it to heat hospitals, schools, and children's nurseries. We have given private apartments and other facilities a lower priority and will cope in other ways. "Reporter: Thank you. There have been reports in the British press about the centres of Omarska and Trnopolje and places like that. Do the authorities in Prijedor have any control, or have they had any control over places like that? "Stakic: These places, such as Omarska, Keraterm, and Trnopolje, were a necessity in a given moment and were formed according to a decision of the civilian authorities in Prijedor. "Reporter: So those three camps, or how are they -- ? "Stakic: Reception centres. "Reporter: -- Reception centres were formed according to the decision of your civilian authorities? "Stakic: Yes, yes. As I have said, this was a necessity at the given moment when there was no longer any possibility to resolve the question of relations and the division of power through agreement, by peaceful means, and when extremists from the ranks of the SDA and the HDZ party, but mostly the SDA, which won here and which at one point lost control and started using force, murdering members of the army and the police. We had to set up such centres. Omarska was an investigation centre where, in a way, a triage was done where 40-odd trained people, who had previously worked as military investigators, or civilian investigators, from the public security station. "Reporter: So Omarska was an investigation centre, you say? "Stakic: Yes. "Reporter: You had 40 trained people, you say, from the army and the police? "Stakic: Inspectors, inspectors, crime inspectors, who did the questioning. While Trnopolje was something quite different. Those people had fled from the ravages of war, from the invasion of those extremists who pushed their own civilians, women and children, in front of weapons and tried with them to breakthrough, to pull out across Kozara. They are even known to have fired at their own column of refugees in Kozara and so on. And we simply received them down there in Trnopolje in order to supply them with food, for them to get international aid, for transport to be organised for them to places where they wished to go, and to protect them from both the Muslim extremists and from revanchism by members of the other peoples who had lost their closest kin, their dearest, to prevent these revanchist relations and further bloodshed among innocent civilians. This all lasted -- Omarska and Keraterm -- for two or three months. Trnopolje, until around mid-September, when it was officially closed. However, politics is again getting entangled in all that. The people from Trnopolje were transferred, let me tell you, under the organisation of the International Red Cross to Karlovac from where they could look for a way to get to third European countries. But the organised part of the SDA that remained in the Prijedor Municipality area called on the remaining Muslim population to come to Trnopolje again, because it now represented a step towards departing for Europe. Fortunately, and with great help from the International Red Cross, which saw that 95 per cent of those who were in Trnopolje now, those who came later, had their family homes, their apartments, and told them that assistance was conditional on their return to their homes. We managed to -- to organise transport for them and take them to their homes and apartments. "Reporter: So the people who were in Trnopolje sometime in early December are now at home? "Stakic: Yes. "Reporter: Are they mostly Muslims or Croats? Who are they? "Stakic: They are mostly Muslims. There are a few Croats, because most Croats live in the town area, in the Ljubija area, in their homes. Most -- A certain number have even responded to the callup to the regular Army of Republika Srpska. They are working, their family members are working, in firms to the extent to which we are working at all, and there have been fewer problems with them. Now, these people have also returned to their homes. The International Red Cross visited me yesterday, and they are in the territory of the municipality today to visit them in their homes so that we can jointly send them certain assistance, that which is their due naturally. "Reporter: Will those Muslims stay here? "Stakic: Those who wish to. A good number of them wish to leave this area, and surprisingly, practically no one -- or better said, perhaps only 1 per cent - wish to go to Alija's so-called independent state, or rather, the territory that is under the control of the Muslim forces. This means that around 99 per cent, or practically 100 per cent, wish to go to Europe. To what extent this is politics is less -- the economic factor is also important here because they know and they hear that up there, they will get some aid in marks, or pounds, or shillings, and so on. They get aid in food. "Reporter: Let me ask you some more questions about interrogations. What was the purpose of the investigations in Omarska? "Stakic: The purpose of the investigations was to identify the most extreme people from the ranks of the SDA and the Muslim population who armed the Muslims, who were the instigators and perpetrators of the entire armed operation of attacks on members of the regular army and police. Because we have never, at any point, not even to this very day, declared war on the entire Muslim people or a struggle for the extermination of that people, but only a struggle against the extremists among that people, those who did not want to coexistence here, who wanted a unitary state with absolute rights for the Muslim people, and with prepared programmes for the extermination of the Serbian people from these areas. You can find documentation on that in the investigation material from that investigation centre at Omarska which was later transferred to Manjaca, and with the corps security of this -- "Reporter: And what happened, then, to the people whom you discovered were responsible? "Stakic: Those most responsible, around 1.350 of them, were transferred to Manjaca, once the military prison at Manjaca was formed. The rest were released, allowed to go home. Some of them later went, with regular documentation and certificates from third countries. We gave them -- enabled them to get all the documents and to leave the territory of Prijedor Municipality and Republika Srpska safely, while some of them, believe me, still live in the territory of Prijedor Municipality today. "Reporter: There have been press reports in the west about mistreatment of people at Omarska. Are you familiar with these reports? "Stakic: I'm not familiar with the kind of reports being referred to. I know about some that, for example - and that is also why I asked you in the beginning for objectiveness, just for objectiveness and not for bias - where a man of 50 kilograms, who is by nature of such constitution, is filmed while standing next to him is a man of 130 kilograms, and the colleague from television did not want to film the latter in order to show the former as not having anything to eat and as not eating. I am a doctor by profession, and theoretically, someone of 100 kilograms could not have come down to 50 in a month and a half or two, even if he had had nothing to eat. Even if he had been on a hunger strike or not been given any food at all. "Reporter: That was shown on television? "Stakic: Yes, it was filmed. I did not get a chance to see it because I often do not get a chance to watch even our own television. "Reporter: He will tell you what the western press said, and you can explain to us what it is about. There have been reports in the western press and on television -- there have been reports in the western press and on television that people were beaten at Omarska. "Stakic: The entire -- representatives of the press and television were absolutely allowed to be present in all these centres and to film and to have interviews. Therefore, they could have filmed that and seen that. I do not have such information. Even if anyone was injured or wounded, that was in the course of battle, and that was the condition that he was brought in up there. That is one thing. However, I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. do not have any information about maltreatment and physical violence in the centres themselves. Our view, the official view of the authorities, was that there must not be any maltreatment, because after all, that was an investigation centre. "Reporter: There have also been reports in the western press and on television based on statements by refugees from these parts that people were killed at Omarska. "Stakic: You have all the data about the number of people who died in these centres, in the public security station. That, too, has happened. And the corpses or the bodies of the dead were sent to their families at their request so they could bury them properly. "Reporter: I'm sorry, I didn't understand that. "Stakic: There were cases, because I was informed, informed by the chief of the service which -- under whose supervision everything proceeded, cases of death which are -- have medical documentation about death, and not about murder. "Reporter: At Omarska? "Stakic: Yes. "Reporter: Do you know how many people that was? "Stakic: I cannot say exactly. It is not a large number. "Reporter: Not many, you say? "Stakic: No. "Reporter: Are you aware that the United States State Department has submitted to the United Nations reports about killings and maltreatment at Omarska? "Stakic: I do not have any such information. I mean, I'm not aware of that. "Reporter: How would you explain to the people in England, to the audience in England, what happened here over the last six months? "Stakic: First of all, I would like to greet viewers in England. For us here, the reports of the London press and television, and especially official London, are a kind of measure of the balance of powers in the world and the situation in the world. However, it is difficult to explain from here what is actually happening here to the people who live in England and on the island, who are an integral part of Europe, but who are nevertheless a little separated from Europe and are quite far from the Balkans. Those of us who have lived here for centuries, I mean the Serbs and the other peoples, I also mean the Muslims, who were created artificially, who were against the Serbs in the two previous wars while the Serbs were on the side of the allies both times, and this was from the very beginning. In other words, not at the very end of the war. What should have been done actually -- a little more time should have been devoted to getting to know the spirit and mentality of this people. Both times, in both world wars, previous wars, we Serbs with our broadmindedness forgave everything, all the crimes that were committed by the Ustashas, mobilised from among the Croatian people and the Muslim people, where we suffered more by their hand than on the hands of fascist Germany, where on Kozara alone, 14.000 children were killed. "Reporter: Where were they killed? "Stakic: In Jasenovac, but the Kozara children in the Jasenovac camp, the concentration camp. And to forgive all that, to agree to live in a new state called democratic by the communists, and Josip Broz, only to have the HDZ appear again with the same symbols that the Ustashas had in 1941, to have the SDA appear and tie its flag in a knot and make a war coalition, the Serbian people could not pass over that because, after all, it was a period of less than 50 years. Fortunately, I do not remember it, but my grandfather died in that war, his brother, my cousin, and many others. Quite simply, I have had the opportunity to spend time in Western Europe. We are a part of Europe only territorially, and even Serbia, which had its own state as far back as the middle ages and its tradition, its culture, its religion, was never, not for a single moment, Greater Serbia. The Serbs have never live together in one state. Out of a human broadmindedness, pan-southern Slavism, we created Yugoslavia so that all the southern Slavs could live in a single state. However, this did not suit someone else. And when Yugoslavia's breakup again, the secession of Slovenia, Croatia, but that part of Croatia where the Croatian people are in a majority, the world should have known, and even the English public and people, that Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is a Yugoslavia in miniature, would suffer the same fate. And not to dwell too much on that, that is now a matter of being familiar with history and, and the times and the territories that we are living in here. "Reporter: Five years ago, could you have imagined that the situation would develop like this, the way it is today? "Stakic: No, I couldn't. And not only because there were no signs of it, but because of my personal upbringing and views. I am against war, against force. I am in favour of reaching an agreement. There were signs of this here back in the 1970s, in 1968, 1972, since the Maspok movement, called Maspok, the mass nationalist movement in Croatia and so on. However, the focus was on resolving economic problems with the help of that national community, that we would overcome that. There was another current among the Muslims as well. "Reporter: Could you please say something, your first and last name only. "Stakic: Okay. "Reporter: On the way here, we drove past Kozarac, and from what we know, there was a big battle in Kozarac. What happened there? "Stakic: That is precisely where that Muslim extremism escalated. Because Kozarac, with its surroundings, had around 20.000 Muslims. And in Kozarac itself, which has between 10 and 12.000, we found original lists with 3 and a half thousand, or to be more precise, 3.791 members of the illegal Muslim Territorial Defence, the number of each gun, and the date on which they were issued, and other light and medium heavy weapons. We had indications that this existed before. However, the fact and the moment when they came out to the Prijedor/Banja Luka main road and blocked around 10 kilometres of the road at the entrance to and exit from their territory, and all local access roads, the army -- actually, we made a decision that the army and the police go up there and lift the blockade of that road and that they withdraw at least 100 metres from the road into the depth of their territory, that nobody would enter deeper into their territory there. But that road not only links these two towns, but even broader, these regions. And at the approach of the first police and military vehicle, they opened fire without warning. After that, clashes followed, and all that happened subsequently. You also saw a large number of destroyed houses and so on. Slowly, life is returning to normal up here, too. We have some people who were up there, who barely managed to survive, who took refuge, and who have now returned. We have a small number of people, refugees from the rest of Bosnia and Herzegovina who fled, and so we offered them accommodation. There are some Croats. There are Ukrainians and Ruthenians, who do not mind anything, either these new authorities or the politics, and who stayed up there to live in their houses. A lot of them have also had their family homes destroyed, and I, as the mayor, and with my executive authority, we are trying to compensate them for this, either with another house or an apartment to secure a roof over their heads. We have managed to repair both the electric power network and the waterworks to such an extent that they may have electricity along with the same power cuts, of course, as the other citizens of Prijedor Municipality. "Reporter: And where are the Muslims who used to live in Kozarac? "Stakic: Well, Trnopolje was mainly filled with Muslims from Kozarac. A good part of those extremists were from Kozarac and they went to Trnopolje. The 1500 and some men who were moved with the help of the International Red Cross to Karlovac were mostly from Kozarac, then comes the reuniting of families in keeping with the Geneva Convention and their families follow them and join them and so on. The rest, because their family homes had been destroyed, were accommodated either in the territory of Prijedor Municipality or went, were transferred to -- some did go to central Bosnia, those who expressed this wish. We organised buses and a train for them, and this was for free just that they go, so that there should be no casualties. So that genocide that we have already been blamed for in Europe should not occur. It is better that they leave and tomorrow, when the war ends and depending on the agreement at the level of the newly formed states, which I am convinced will be created in this territory, those among them who want to return here will be able to do so. "Reporter: What would you say to the Muslims who fled from Kozarac and who are now in Europe? "Stakic: To wait for the war. They are on one hand fortunate because they have avoid the ravages of war and all these shortages and poverty that we have. And regardless of how this is resolved, I mean at the level, up there at the higher level, the interstate or intercantonal level, however Bosnia and Herzegovina is finally divided, we in Prijedor will respect all agreements. "Reporter: Do you think they will come back? "Stakic: I don't know. But depending on their wish, if they wish to return, they will be enabled to do so. "Reporter: There has been a lot of talk in the western press about something called ethnic cleansing. What is your response to that? "Stakic: It is not -- not good for, for me as the president of Prijedor Municipality to name the municipalities of Bugojno, Vitez, Travnik, and Zenica. Some are controlled by the HVO, the Croatian defence council, and others by the Muslims forces. Serbian citizens who have been expelled brutally from their houses and apartments with bundles in their hands are coming to me from these territories and nobody in the west mentions that as ethnic cleansing. While in Prijedor, where we are struggling to -- merely to secure the papers for them and a accident departure at their personal wish and request, that is being called ethnic cleansing. Secondly, a certain number of Muslims are still in Prijedor. There are those who are employed, I mean, in the public services sector and the economy, even though it is operating at 10 to 15 per cent of its full capacity which you can see for yourself. Feel free to take a walk through the enterprises. And I think that that remark is not well-intentioned. I have already said at the beginning that most of them are leaving now partly for political reasons, but more for economic reasons, because we are currently all endangered here. I once had a salary equivalent to a thousand German marks. Now, as the mayor, I have sixty marks. And I am a subtenant, and my wife is unemployed and so on. So that these -- not only the Muslims are endangered here. And let me tell you, too, that nearly all your questions about -- except for the general ones, what is happening in Prijedor and what it is like -- mainly show an interest in the Muslim part of the population. We also have a Croatian part. A good number of whom have responded to the callup, to the Army of Republika Srpska, and to the police and who have accepted the authorities, and we have had seven and a half thousand refugees since a year and a half ago who fled from Slovenia and Croatia, mostly from Croatia, and more than 10.000 refugees in Prijedor from Bosnia and Herzegovina, the part that is under the control of Croatian and Muslims forces. "Reporter: Are the High Commissariat for refugees and the International Red Cross giving you the help that you need to resettle these people, the refugees from other parts of Bosnia and Yugoslavia? "Stakic: Both these institutions are giving us aid. Now, whether it is what is needed, let me say immediately that it is not. I told the representatives of both institutions this, because our needs are much greater. However, these two institutions are really helping us at this moment. And thanks to the fact that they have deigned to come to the municipality at all, to meet the representatives of the authorities, approximately two months ago, that cooperation is much better, and that aid, to the satisfaction of both sides, I apologise for speaking on their behalf as well, is now being monitored much more efficiently, how it is distributed, how much is coming in and so on. And I am using this opportunity to thank both organisations for their help and their will to help. Or as their representatives say, they are willing to help and are themselves aware that they are not in a position to resolve all our problems. But for the moment, we are satisfied with that, with their will and their presence. And this goes back, as I have said, over the past few months, even though we've had refugees in the territory of Prijedor Municipality for the last year and a half. "Reporter: What do the Serbian refugees, their children and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. women, what do they need most for the coming winter? "Stakic: We have some refugees here, a smaller part, from the Velika Kladusa municipality, the Cazin region, who managed to pull out through the Knin Krajina and to bring a part of their assets with them, from furniture to food and so on. But the majority is from the rest of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they literally came with bundles in their hand. And they need everything. But their most essential need is for stoves, ordinary stoves for heating. We can provide firewood for them. There is firewood. They need food. They need clothing and footwear, especially for children, I mean, and they need medicines. They are most essential, but they literally need everything. "Reporter: How have the people in Prijedor received the refugees who have come here? "Stakic: They receive them with all that - perhaps this is a little boastful - with all that Krajina hospitality, and they are helping as much as they are able to help at this moment, with surplus food, surplus clothing, by giving them a bed to sleep in, a place to spend the night for a few days, and even longer until we accommodate them in dormitories and schools. And sometimes we even put them up in ruined houses and help them to recover and survive this winter. "Reporter: Are you a busy man? "Stakic: Very busy. I work as much as 16, 18, even 20 hours a day. And being 30 years old, I think that in the past six months to a year, I have aged more than five years. I feel so tired and... "Reporter: Do you think of the future? "Stakic: My own or that of the state? The state. "Reporter: How do you see things in Prijedor in five or ten years from now? "Stakic: Well, all the same, Prijedor is participating in this war, and a part of its people are participating in the war even though here there is no war currently in the territory itself. And I personally think that reinforcing the corridor, our link with the Republic of Yugoslavia itself, which is our only way out into the world for the time being, because we are blocked from all other sides, I think that that in itself will bring the war to an end, regardless of the fact that there will be sabotage, killings, and breakthrough attempts and attacks along the lines of separation. I would like to stress here that, in my opinion, and I am a small man from a small municipality, especially looking at Europe and the world, the international factor can play an important role. I think that from the beginning, the entire concept of influence on everything that is happening in Yugoslavia was a little crooked. But it is never too late to correct that. An equally objective view needs to be taken of all the participants in the war here. If Croatia were publicly to admit that it has so many brigades and so many troops engaged in Bosnia and Herzegovina, nobody in the world would condemn that. But they condemn Serbia, on whose borders with Bosnia and Herzegovina there are both border guards and members of international organisations. And they see that there are no members of the Serbian army, I mean, the Army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in these parts. But it is still being accused and penalized and so on. Still, I think that if the war stops and if these areas here are allowed to do business and cooperate economically with the rest of Europe and the world, without Alija's signature and to have more regular electricity supplies, we will very soon come to a position to resolve our problems, our problems of survival for ourselves. "Reporter: Thank you very much. I'd like to ask you two things: First, is there anything that we have not talked about that you would like to tell viewers in England? "Stakic: Well, I would like -- "Reporter: Let me ask the question. What is it that you would like to tell people in England? "Stakic: Besides having already greeted them, I personally still count on the objectivity of the English population, the English people, which I have already mentioned, and simply that any report in the newspapers and on television is not enough in itself to understand the people of an area requires knowledge of a little of the history of that -- these people. And what is most pressing for us at this moment is that aid in food and medicines and the influence, as much as possible, of public opinion in England on these international organisations, to lift the blockade of these parts. What I mean to say is that so that our economic organisations can do business and cooperate with firms and economic organisations in Europe and the world normally, as all the others do, without an embargo, without pressure. Because we are now asked strictly to have the consent of Alija's government in order to be able to export or import certain goods. And you know that we are at present enemies. Whether we want to admit it or not, we are on two warring sides, on two sides of the front. "Reporter: Thank you very much."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you for this. Finally, may we hear, what about the witness of Monday, the witness to come? Any proofing notes, any exhibit lists?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I think the proofing notes were provided previously, because this was a witness who was scheduled earlier. But I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Could you please give us, first of all, the number, the degree of protection, that we are prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It's 65 ter number 43, 4-3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: 4-3. Yes. May we ask you that in case --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just for the Court's -- the witness actually, because the witness was here previously and a representative from the office, Mr. Waidyaratne, spoke to her previously, he actually won't have any chance to speak to her before she testifies. But he may have previously provided proofing notes. I don't recall that myself, whether he did or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If you could please be so kind and check, and in case there is any additional information also on exhibits, please inform us. Any other observations by the parties? This seems not to be the case. Case manager OTP gives us a hint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The message I received is that Ms. Korner suggests -- asked the Court if the Court wants to read documents tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think if there is no necessity seen by the parties - from our side, there is no such one - then unfortunately we have to state that as to the lack of evidence provided by the OTP, we can't have a hearing tomorrow. And the trial stands, therefore, adjourned until Monday, 9.00. This concludes the 47th day of the hearing.
